articles.title: A US$1.13m Magikarp? This fish began as a fan-club prize
articles.summary: A 600-point Fan Club reward now carries a US$1,131,095 auction total. See the actual slab, the original prize page and the premium behind the number. Alt still marks the lot Pending.
articles.imageAlt: The actual Japanese Shining Magikarp 600-point Fan Club PSA 10 slab, cert 19421750, photographed by Alt, beside the house headline The Fan Club Fish.
articles.imageCaption: The actual 600-point Fan Club Magikarp offered in Alt’s 5 November auction, PSA 10 cert 19421750.

sections.heading: A golden fish, a seven-figure headline
sections.html:
THE QUICK TAKE

Alt’s 5 November auction page displays US$1,131,095 for a Japanese Shining Magikarp Fan Club promo, PSA 10, cert 19421750. The figure includes a 20% buyer’s premium. The lot is still marked Pending at our 7 November check.

The photograph shows a small gold fish swimming through blue water. The story behind it runs from an old Japanese fan-club rewards scheme to the top end of Pokémon auctions. The exact printing—and the exact meaning of the price—matter.

sections.heading: Which Magikarp? Start with this slab
sections.html:
This is the Japanese 600-point Fan Club Shining Magikarp, illustrated by Ken Sugimori. Alt lists 34 bids. That is a count of bids, not a count of different bidders.

The Fan Club printing has embossed foil on Magikarp and no rarity symbol. Those details distinguish it from the regular Japanese set version. Fanatics’s printing description ↗

sections.heading: Before the auction, there were GET points
sections.html:
Members earned GET points through club activities, including tournaments and magazine contributions. The reward catalogue in Trainers Vol. 11 shows Shining Magikarp as Prize G: 600 points. The panel below is an excerpt from that original page, preserved in Pokumon’s archive.

Fanatics and Heritage catalogue the reward’s distribution from May 2001 to December 2002. It belonged to a system that rewarded taking part in the hobby. That history gives collectors something beyond a familiar character and a shiny finish. It does not tell us how many copies were originally distributed. Heritage’s historical description ↗

sections.heading: US$942,579 becomes US$1,131,095
sections.html:
Alt’s bid-history panel shows a highest bid of US$942,579. Its published fee rule adds 20%. That contributes about US$188,516 to the displayed total.

ComponentUS dollarsBasis
Highest displayed bid942,579.00Alt bid history
20% buyer premium188,515.80Calculated
Calculated total1,131,094.80Before rounding
Displayed auction total1,131,095Alt lot page

Download the dated auction data (CSV) · Download the calculation graphic (SVG)

Pending is not proof of a payment problem. Alt gives auction purchases of US$10,000 or more up to five days for payment and describes holds for wires in transit. We have no settlement receipt or confirmed definition of this lot’s Pending label. Alt’s payment terms ↗

sections.heading: An earlier PSA 10 adds context
sections.html:
A different copy of the same printing, PSA 10 cert 77121318, sold through the auction platform now called Fanatics Collect for US$49,200 including buyer’s premium. Its own page dates that sale 19 July 2024.

Lot / certOriginal-platform dateUSD incl. premiumStatus
Fanatics / 7712131819 July 202449,200Sold
Alt / 194217505 November 20261,131,095Pending on 7 Nov

These are two dated lot records, not a price index or a demonstrated return available to every owner. PSA currently lists 19 examples in grade 10. Population is a grading record; it is not the print run or a count of every surviving card. Check the exact PSA entry ↗

THE VERDICT

The compelling detail is the journey from participation reward to trophy-card auction. Keep the printing, certificate, buyer premium and Pending status together. A seven-figure headline earns a closer look at the actual fish.

articles.title: Best Binder for Pokémon Cards: Why I Use the Vault X XL
articles.summary: My old Jordan cards got a little too attached to their binder. Here’s why I chose the 624-card Vault X XL for Pokémon, with real photos, Amazon prices and sleeve-fit comparisons.
articles.imageAlt: The black Vault X XL zip binder with a green zip pull, framed in BuyTrigger.Cards ink and red.
articles.imageCredit: Product photography: Vault X, 12-pocket XL catalogue. Review graphic: BuyTrigger.Cards.
articles.imageCaption: The exact 624-card XL model reviewed here.

sections.heading: My pick, in one minute
sections.html:
MY PICK: VAULT X XL

624 slots. Comfortable with my penny sleeves. A binder I actually like carrying. I paid £30.99, and I’d buy it again.

Best binder for Pokémon cards? Of the ones I’ve tried, the Vault X 12-pocket XL is my favourite. The look matters to me. So does being able to move a sleeved card without holding my breath. But the reason I take all this seriously starts with my old basketball collection.

I bought this binder myself. Vault X has not sponsored this review. These are ordinary product links; this review earns no Amazon commission.

sections.heading: Thirty-five years. A little too attached.
sections.html:
Some of my Jordan cards got stuck to the pages of an old binder.

Thirty-five years together. Apparently, they took the commitment seriously.

It sounds funny until you’re looking at the card. I’d kept that Ultra PRO binder for about 35 years. For roughly the first 25, it seemed fine. Over the next ten, the pages started giving me problems. Those cards weren’t in separate penny sleeves.

I don’t know exactly what those old pages were made from or why the sticking happened. I do know how it feels to look at cards you’ve kept for years and wish you’d paid more attention to the storage.

That’s the feeling behind this review. When I put Pokémon cards away now, I’m thinking about the person opening that binder in another 35 years. I’d quite like him to be pleased with me.

sections.heading: Why I went XL
sections.html:
In October 2026, I returned a black Vault X 480-card strap binder that cost £16.99 and bought the 624-card XL zip binder for £30.99.

The difference was £14. That bought the larger zip format and another 144 slots: 30% more capacity. For the way I want to keep growing my collection, that was an easy upgrade to justify.

Those are my actual purchase prices. The 624-card XL and standard 480-card zip binder are different models, so check the capacity before you click. “Black Vault X binder” isn’t quite specific enough.

sections.heading: The bits I actually care about
sections.html:
Yes, I care how it looks. I recognise Vault X from card shows, and I’d rather walk in carrying one than an unknown brand. The aesthetics and branding are part of why I chose it. We spend all this time admiring the cards; I’m allowed to like the thing I carry them in.

My penny-sleeved cards fit comfortably. I returned an Ultimate Guard binder because it felt too tight with the sleeves I used. With my Vault X, cards go in and out easily. Putting a card away should not feel like a difficult parking manoeuvre. I don’t have the model name for the Ultimate Guard I returned; fit also depends on your sleeves.

No weird plastic smell. Mine doesn’t have it. A small pleasure, perhaps, but I notice it every time I open a binder.

I check the materials now. Vault X lists archival-safe, acid-free and PVC-free materials, side-loading pockets and a zip closure. Its cover is described as water-resistant, rather than waterproof. Those are useful specifications to check, not a promise that any binder will last forever. XL specifications

One thing I had to correct while researching this: Ultra PRO says it introduced PVC-free card pages in 1988. So I can’t blame the age of my old binder and call its chemistry solved. Modern Ultra PRO Vivid binders also advertise acid-free, non-PVC materials. Ultra PRO’s history

sections.heading: Does the price stack up?
sections.html:
Here’s the useful surprise: my preferred binder isn’t the most expensive one in this comparison.

These are Amazon UK displayed item prices checked on 7 November 2026, for the selected black zip-binder listings. The capacities differ, which is why I’ve included the cost per 100 slots.

BinderListed capacityAmazon item priceCost per 100 slots
Vault X 12-pocket XL624£30.99£4.97
Card Guardian 12-pocket480£24.99£5.21
Ultra PRO Vivid 12-pocket480£33.95£7.07
Gamegenic Zip-Up 24-pocket480£32.99£6.87
Ultimate Guard Zipfolio 480480Buying options only—

The XL is £6 more than Card Guardian, with 144 more slots. It is £2 below the selected Gamegenic listing and £2.96 below Ultra PRO. At those prices, the premium-looking choice also gives me a competitive cost per slot. I’ll happily take that.

Prices exclude sleeves and delivery. Offers can change; checkout was not completed. Ultimate Guard showed buying options without one clear selected total, so I’ve left its price blank. The Gamegenic “24-pocket” name counts both sides of a page; its total is 480 slots. Gamegenic specifications

sections.heading: What Amazon buyers said
sections.html:
My own tight-pocket experience made sleeve-fit complaints worth reading. We checked positive feedback as well as critical reviews across all five listings. Vault X gets the same scrutiny here.

BinderWhy people consider itWhat the customer-review check found
Vault X XLMy preferred look and penny-sleeve fit; the pooled listing is strongly positive overall.The black XL filter included reports of page separation, fragile pocket seams and page bowing. Inspect the copy you receive.
Ultimate Guard ZipfolioBuyers praise its finish, zip and capacity; some report good double/triple-sleeve fit.A January 2022 buyer reported Ultra PRO penny sleeves would not fit an older royal-blue version, unlike their teal version. Other reports mention pocket defects or zipper issues.
Ultra PRO VividA current acid-free, non-PVC zip binder; positive feedback on sleeved access.The listing had 53 global ratings and no critical written reviews returned by this filter. Its 480 slots offer less capacity than the XL.
Gamegenic Zip-UpBuyers like the feel and zip; rated for 480 sleeved cards.Several 2024–25 buyers reported internal page colours differing from listing photos. One black-variant buyer reported looser pockets than a previous purchase.
Card GuardianLower item price; many buyers praise the build and value.Several 2023–24 reports describe uneven or tight top/bottom pockets with sleeved cards. Others are satisfied with sleeve fit.

That table is other buyers’ feedback. Amazon groups colours, models and older versions, so look closely at the variant being reviewed. My practical check is simple: try your actual sleeves in the binder you receive, and inspect the pockets and seams before filling it.

sections.heading: XL—or a smaller Vault X?
sections.html:
The XL in the name is doing real work. Vault X lists it at about 350 × 340 mm. Check your bag and shelf. A good binder is less convenient if you have to buy it its own furniture.

12-pocket XL, 624 cards: my choice for a growing collection. See the exact XL on Amazon.

9-pocket zip, 360 cards: a smaller format if the XL is more binder than you need. See the black 9-pocket on Amazon.

4-pocket zip, 160 standard-size cards: a compact option for a focused selection. The prepared listing is Teal. See the standard-card 4-pocket on Amazon.

These are standard-card zip binders. The newer hard-holder product is a different review for another day. Always check the model, dimensions and sleeve fit.

sections.heading: Would I buy it again?
sections.html:
Yes. I like looking at it, carrying it and using it. My sleeves fit, my collection has room, and the stated materials are what I want to see now.

If I want my Pokémon cards around for another 35 years, saving a few pounds on the binder isn’t the part of the hobby I’m going to turn into an extreme sport.

No binder can guarantee a grade, a future price or 35 years of perfect condition. Good sleeves, gentle handling, suitable storage and checking the pages still matter. But I’d rather make a careful choice now than have another awkward reunion with an old card.

MY VERDICT

For my collection, the Vault X XL is the best binder I’ve used so far. I’d buy it again.

articles.title: She queued from 5am for Pokémon—and got the LAST box
articles.summary: Seven UPCs. A 5am start. Tanja got the last one, and her cat stole the photo. Inside the queues, first-pack joy and sweet little trades of Pokémon release day.
articles.imageAlt: A credited photo collage of the Best Buy umbrella queue, Tanja’s black cat and Day UPC, and Lain’s Zorua and Spritzee cards.
articles.imageCaption: Original collector photographs: the queue, the last box and the cards behind a kind trade.

sections.heading: 5am. Seven boxes. One last UPC.
sections.html:
THE RELEASE-DAY ALBUM

The last box, an umbrella queue, a first-pack surprise and a trade between two people who knew each other’s favourites. Six collectors’ accounts bring the 6 November Pokémon launch weekend into focus.

Tanja says she joined the queue at 5am. The shop had seven Ultra-Premium Collections. She got the last one.

Her photograph gives the story an excellent supporting character: a black cat, stretched across the foreground while the Espeon-fronted Day box sits behind it. The box has made it into the picture. So has the cat.

In a follow-up reply, Tanja said the stock count was announced when the shop opened, after people had already been waiting for hours. She also described the six people ahead of her as fans who planned to open their boxes.

For everyone still waiting, there was a familiar calculation: how much time to give the hunt, and whether there would still be a box when their turn came. Read Tanja’s follow-up ↗

sections.heading: Under the umbrellas, the queue kept going
sections.html:
Luckstruck9’s photograph looks down a wet pavement outside Best Buy. Umbrellas punctuate the line; the shop’s signs run above it. The poster said the doors were still about 40 minutes from opening.

This was their first Pokémon TCG line wait. They said they had checked Target shortly after it opened and missed the 30th products, then tried Best Buy. Their post mixes determination with doubt about how difficult even casual collecting can feel.

The photograph is evidence of one busy shop visit. It also gives a release announcement something a product render cannot: the weather, the waiting and the people who have organised part of their day around a pack of cards.

sections.heading: The opening could wait for a cousin
sections.html:
For Lalo A. Vera, posting as bplobo8 on Threads, the hunt was also a family errand. In an earlier post, Lalo described an overnight wait. In the follow-up, they explained that working nights made the hours easier to manage, although the weather still made itself felt.

“for myself and my cousin”

Lalo A. Vera / @bplobo8, explaining who the purchase was for.

At the time of that reply, the packs were still unopened. Lalo said they would be opened the next day. There was somebody else to share the moment with.

Lalo also described finding friendly people in a community that, in their view, often gets a bad reputation. At that point, the opening was still ahead of them: a purchase made for two people, with the moment saved for later. Lalo’s account ↗

sections.heading: Zorua for Spritzee: a very good little trade
sections.html:
Lain went to a card shop with their girlfriend, picked up a cute Altaria and bought Delta Reign packs. Their post reports a Mega Rayquaza and a Zorua pull. Then comes the detail that gives the whole outing its charm: Lain traded the Zorua to their girlfriend for Spritzee because she loves Zorua.

The Rayquaza pictured is the regular Mega Rayquaza ex, 084/103. Here, the important match was between a favourite Pokémon and the person who wanted it.

Two collectors were making their own collections a little more personal. The detail worth remembering is that one knew exactly which Pokémon the other loved.

sections.heading: One first pack, one very welcome Raikou
sections.html:
Lox was having a difficult day. According to their post, their very first pack of the newly released Delta Reign contained Raikou ex Special Illustration Rare. The surprise was welcome.

The photo shows the actual English card in a holder. The first-pack detail comes from Lox’s account; one fortunate opening says nothing about the odds for the next person. As a release-day moment, though, it is wonderfully easy to understand: opening a pack and finding something that improves your day.

sections.heading: Delta first. Anniversary box later.
sections.html:
TVA Friend’s photograph has room for both launches: a Day anniversary UPC beside a Delta Reign Elite Trainer Box, with boosters and other pickups spread below. Asked which came first, the collector replied: “Delta first, 30th later.”

The distinction is useful for anyone following the weekend through a feed of similar boxes. The Day UPC belongs to 30th Celebration; Delta Reign is a separate expansion. The collector’s follow-up ↗

sections.heading: One weekend, several ways into the hobby
sections.html:
These accounts span different shops, products and local circumstances. Elsewhere in our community replies, one collector reported an ETB on a regular Target shelf; another found packs behind the till at a Morrisons petrol station. Those are individual visits, not promises of stock at another branch.

CollectorThe moment they reported
Tanja5am queue; last of seven UPCs
Luckstruck9Umbrella queue; about 40 minutes before Best Buy opened
LaloPurchase for themselves and a cousin; opening saved for later
LainZorua traded for Spritzee with their girlfriend
LoxRaikou ex SIR reported in the first pack
TVA FriendDelta queue first; anniversary products later

Online orders have their own timetable. Pokémon Center’s shipment table, checked on 7 November, estimates mid-November for selected Delta Reign products in the US, Canada and UK. That estimate concerns the listed products and channel; it is not a new date for every shop. Official shipment estimates ↗

Public posts naturally favour the exceptional wait, the big haul and the lucky pull. These are individual snapshots of a much larger weekend. The queues were real. So were the cat cameo, the family plan and the favourite-card trade.

THE MOMENT TO KEEP

Lain’s Zorua-for-Spritzee swap is the detail to take away: knowing what somebody else loves, then helping them get it. Release day can leave you with a card, a story and somebody to share it with.

What was your moment? Tell @buytriggercards who you opened with, what you found, or which small trade made the day.

Reporting note: based on the collectors’ public posts and follow-up replies, checked 6–7 November. Purchase, wait and pull accounts are attributed to their authors. Photos retain creator credit and links to the posts being discussed. We did not attend these queues or conduct in-person interviews.

sections.heading: The country drop dates
sections.html:
THE QUICK TAKE

Australia’s reported launch is 5 November, two days after Canada and five days before the confirmed US launch. New Zealand is already advertising the toys. The UK and Ireland have a February 2027 window. The dates below separate official announcements from original store reporting.

MarketDrop dateEvidence
Canada3 November 2026Reported
PokéBeach store reporting ↗
Australia5 November 2026Reported
PokéBeach store reporting ↗
United States10 November 2026Official
McDonald’s ↗

The useful dates are 3, 5 and 10 November. PokéBeach reports Canada’s 3 November start and Australia’s 5 November start after speaking to multiple stores. McDonald’s USA directly confirms 10 November. Those sources give us actual days to put on a calendar.

The evidence differs, so the chart keeps that difference visible: Canada and Australia are reported exact dates; the US is official. Canada is already running according to Pokémon’s 3 November notice, which gives a 30 November finish. That newer official ending replaces the older reported 7 December date.

Official McDonald’s pages in Australia and New Zealand also advertise the Pokémon toys as available. They supply no launch day. That supports a current availability label; Australia’s exact 5 November date still comes from store reporting, while New Zealand’s start day remains open.

sections.heading: Europe gets four different months
sections.html:
France and Spain sit in the November group; Germany and the Netherlands in December; Italy in January; the UK and Ireland in February. The current official schedule names 66 markets: 7 in November, 36 in December, 21 in January and 2 in February.

These are launch windows, not restaurant stock counts. An exact day found for the US cannot be copied into the French or Spanish row. The lookup below shows what each source actually establishes.

Pokémon: current global Happy Meal schedule ↗

sections.heading: What is inside—and what changes by region
sections.html:
The miniature Happy Meal boxes are the draw: Pikachu, Eevee, Umbreon and more, with 15 toy designs to collect. The standard announcement pairs one toy with two Pokémon TCG cards from a 15-card set, including seven foil designs.

Quebec has a sticker and four-card booster instead of the miniature toy. That makes a Canadian unboxing location-specific. Seven foil designs is a set count; it is not a published probability of pulling Pikachu.

Pokémon: current global Happy Meal schedule ↗ · Pokémon: Canada promotion and Quebec exception ↗

sections.heading: Beware the older calendar
sections.html:
Nine Asian markets shown in older versions are absent from the current official list. Brunei, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, Pakistan, Singapore and Vietnam previously appeared in December; the Philippines and Thailand in January. PTCG News documents the revision. Their current dates remain unconfirmed here; the omission does not prove cancellation.

Japan’s August 2026 Happy Set was a separate toy and smartphone campaign, with no weekend card gifts. Old Japanese Pikachu pictures and overseas launch clips cannot establish your local card release.

sections.heading: A digital opening, then a physical release
sections.html:
TCG Live is scheduled to receive the expansion at 17:00 GMT on Thursday, 5 November. The official forum notice lists the new packs, code redemption, Battle Pass and Build & Battle event. These are digital milestones; a code becoming redeemable tells us nothing about a UK retailer’s shelf.

The physical set follows on Friday. Mega Rayquaza ex returns alongside three other Mega Evolution Pokémon ex. The expansion also introduces Legendary Stadiums made from two paired Stadium cards. Pokémon says a booster containing one includes both halves. Which illustrated cards turn up in a particular unopened box remains unknown.

That is why this chart has no projected zero-backlog date. Extending the last line segment would assume that arrivals and output keep behaving in the same way. The tracker supplies a history of reported queue sizes, not the inputs for that forecast.

articles.title: Same artwork. A different market.
articles.summary: Same artwork can lead to different prices. Start with the language and exact printing, then check supply, condition and the market where you would sell.

sections.heading: The quick take
sections.html:
THE QUICK TAKE

Match the issue before comparing the price.

Language, set, collector number and grade belong in the comparison. Shared artwork is the beginning of the research.

sections.heading: The picture is familiar. The issue still matters.
Check the identity first
sections.html:
A Japanese card and an English card can share artwork while trading in different markets. Record the language, set, collector number, finish and grade before comparing prices. The English Umbreon reference above shows what an exact identity looks like; it is not a Japanese price comparison.

A reference scan helps identify a printing. It does not show the condition of a particular copy offered for sale. Ask for original front and back photographs before judging centring, corners, edges or surface.

sections.heading: Supply has more than one language
sections.html:
1Same artwork

Check which other-language releases carry it.

2Actual availability

Look at current listings and completed sales in the relevant market.

3Graded population

PSA counts graded examples; raw cards and unopened product remain outside that count.

Review where the artwork appears across English, Japanese and other-language releases. Check observed availability and announced products, and keep those two things separate. Difficult pulls from one English set do not, on their own, establish worldwide artwork scarcity.

A population report answers a narrower question: how many examples a grader has recorded at each grade. It does not count every raw copy still in binders, shops or unopened product.

sections.heading: Bring the price back to your market
sections.html:
For an overseas listing, record the source currency and the full delivered entry, including the applicable shipping, handling, tax and currency-conversion costs. An attractive yen headline can change considerably by arrival.

Then examine recent exact Japanese-card sales where you expect to sell. A few exceptional transactions are different evidence from a regular flow of buyers. Thin sales and stale guides should remain visible.

CheckKeep with the comparison
EntryAvailable copy + delivered cost + source currency
ExitExact issue and grade + recent completed sales
EvidenceSale date, original URL and any uncertainty

sections.heading: The verdict
sections.html: A lower foreign-language price is a lead, not a finished valuation. Match the exact issue, investigate global same-art supply and check attainable local exits. When evidence is thin, keep researching rather than filling the gap with a confident buy label.

sections.heading: The quick take
sections.html:
THE QUICK TAKE

Identify the box before comparing the price.

The 23 October showcase described five configurations. They carry different pack counts and extras, so a cheaper headline does not settle the comparison.

sections.heading: Two boxes that are easy to confuse
sections.html:

sections.heading: What the announcement establishes
sections.html:
Pokémon’s UK showcase dated the physical expansion for 6 November and described more than 135 cards. The table reproduces its announced pack quantities; promos, accessories and decks remain separate parts of the configuration.

A count of packs is useful for identifying a listing. It does not establish the box’s retail price, local stock, pull odds, print run or expected resale outcome. Check a current retailer notice separately before travelling.

sections.heading: Choose the collecting job
sections.html:
1Opening packs

Compare pack quantity with the complete delivered price.

2Chasing the included promo

Match the exact edition and any stamp; do not treat both ETBs as interchangeable.

3Starting a game

Look at the included deck and play accessories, not just the pack count.

A useful product comparison starts with the exact box and edition. Write those down before looking at a seller’s headline price. Otherwise, a cheaper-looking listing can appear to beat a product that includes different contents.

Then separate your reason for wanting it. Someone interested in an included promo is answering a different question from someone who wants packs for a family opening session or a ready-made starting point for play. A single “best value” label can hide those differences.

For a watchlist, we would keep a product’s announcement date, intended release date, edition and contents together. A later retailer check should add its own date and delivered price rather than silently replacing the original announcement. That makes it possible to see what was promised and what subsequently appeared.

The same discipline belongs in the TCG Modern Index: identify the exact collectible before measuring anything. A release headline can explain the calendar; it cannot supply missing transaction data or prove that a card has become undervalued.

sections.heading: The verdict
sections.html: There is no single best box without a purpose and a real price. Match the exact configuration first, then check availability and your reason for choosing it. Our newer Friday/UPC Feature adds the UK calendar distinctions.

Look at the artwork at a completely different scale.

A board and a trading card still need their own identities. Shared art does not make the merchandise a card-index constituent or make their prices directly comparable.

articles.title: Pocket’s proposed six-week rhythm puts collecting pace in focus
articles.summary: The October producer letter proposed a slower pack cycle and more activities between releases. A picture-led guide to the plan and its collecting consequences.
articles.dateNote: Reports the 15 October producer letter as an announcement. Individual feature availability was not rechecked in the game.

sections.heading: The quick take
sections.html:
THE QUICK TAKE

More breathing room was the plan.

The October letter proposed roughly six weeks between new booster releases, with more activities between them. The actual rewards and requirements still determine how collecting feels.

sections.heading: Read the change as a dated plan
What was proposed
sections.html:
The Operations Team’s 15 October letter discussed a new series planned for late October. Alongside the longer cycle, it described dual-type Pokémon, collection-mission immersive rewards and a First Partners special pack with weekly stamina recovery.

It also proposed Community Decks, easier unlimited-use rental decks and improvements for finding trading partners’ missing cards and wishlists. Development details and timing were subject to change; this article reports the letter rather than independently confirming every feature’s rollout.

sections.heading: Use the space between packs
sections.html:
1Choose one goal

A favourite illustration, a collection page or a playable deck is a clearer goal than everything at once.

2Check the requirements

Look at the actual missions, rewards and available cards before deciding whether completion is practical.

3Separate digital from physical

A Pocket change does not establish a paper-card print run or a graded-card price.

The appeal of a collection is often the small, visible goal: finish a favourite Pokémon’s page, find one particular illustration, or build a deck that actually works. A release calendar can support those goals, but a longer interval alone does not tell us how easy completion will become. The rewards, requirements and actual experience still matter.

For a family collection, a simple wishlist can be more useful than another ranking. Separate the cards you like looking at from the ones needed for play, then choose one achievable goal for the next session. That leaves room to enjoy a new card without treating every unfinished set as a problem.

Our desk will keep digital collecting stories distinct from paper-card market research. A popular Pocket illustration can be a good conversation starter; it is not automatically a price signal for a physical card with similar art. That connection needs its own evidence before it belongs in the TCG Modern Index discussion.

sections.heading: The verdict
sections.html: A longer proposed cycle can give a collection more room. Judge the actual missions and collecting experience as they arrive. Keep the October plan, later implementation and physical-card market claims as separate facts.

Enjoy the pictures. Ask questions of the numbers.

sections.html:
Pokémon is at the centre of this project, with room for other cards and the anime we enjoy. The cartoon collectors are our brand characters. Their presence is not a claim that a pictured scene or outing happened.

The point is to make the hobby easier to follow: see the artwork clearly, find the original announcement and understand what sits behind a quoted price.

Open a card for its catalogue picture, exact issue and dated history.

2Catch up

Raw, PSA 9 and PSA 10 are different outcomes, not three amounts to add together. A market guide is different from a verified individual sale. Missing history remains a gap and an older observation keeps its original date.

The public publication is free to read. The My collection link leads to a separate private owner tracker; it is not a public account-signup route. Advertising and affiliate links keep their own labels.

articles.title: A PSA 10 price is not your profit.
articles.summary: The $100 headline becomes $16.01 in our hypothetical example. See how the costs and a lower grade change what remains.

sections.heading: The quick take
sections.html:
THE QUICK TAKE

The sale price is the beginning of the calculation.

A $100 PSA 10 exit leaves $16.01 in our labelled example. A different grade, selling fee or route cost changes the result.

sections.heading: Start with the money committed
sections.html:
1Delivered entry

What the actual card costs to arrive.

2Grading journey

Service fee, shipping, insurance, handling and applicable taxes.

3Selling costs

Marketplace/payment charges and any cost needed to complete the exit.

sections.heading: Three outcomes, counted separately
sections.html:
Raw, PSA 9 and PSA 10 are alternatives for one card. The raw route avoids the grading bill; the graded routes carry it even when the result disappoints. Keep one currency and the exchange-rate date with the calculation.

The chart uses $19 entry, $39.99 grading, $10 other grading-related costs and a 15% selling charge. These are teaching inputs, not a live quote for the pictured cards.

sections.heading: Then lower the exit
sections.html:
With a 10% lower sale and the same costs, the hypothetical PSA 10 profit falls to $7.51 and PSA 9 falls to a $30.74 loss. Graded capital committed in this model is $68.99. The attractive-looking gross sale is much larger than the money left over.

A photograph can start a condition review. It cannot promise the eventual grade, and a seller’s description is not PSA’s own standard. Missing front/back or surface evidence remains a reason to ask for more information.

sections.heading: The verdict
sections.html: Compare the net result at more than one grade before treating a price gap as an opportunity. Change the example’s inputs in the calculator. An attractive PSA 10 price alone does not establish a profitable purchase.

articles.title: Under $20. A $100 PSA 10. Is there actually a deal?
articles.summary: A cheap Raw price and a much higher PSA 10 reference can hide a loss at PSA 9. Four visual checks and the complete hypothetical cost model.

sections.heading: The quick take
sections.html:
THE QUICK TAKE

A five-times price gap can still leave a weak result.

The $19-to-$100 example is a research prompt, not a passing purchase. Look at the available copy, actual exits, lower-grade downside and full cost.

sections.heading: Four gates before a shortlist
sections.html:
1Available entry

Use a real available copy and its delivered cost.

2Exact exit evidence

Match issue, language, variant, grader and grade; separate completed sales from asks and guides.

3PSA 9 downside

Calculate what remains after all grading and selling costs if the result is one grade lower.

4Copy quality

Review original fronts, backs, edges, corners and surface. Missing views are missing evidence.

sections.heading: Why the example fails
A gross multiple hides the capital
sections.html:
The hypothetical PSA 10 sale is about 5.3 times the $19 entry, but that comparison omits grading, related costs and selling charges. The model commits $68.99 before the graded exit. A $16.01 profit is roughly 23% of that capital; the $7.51 stressed result is roughly 11%.

The hypothetical PSA 9 case loses money. That combination fails a demanding downside-and-return screen even though the raw-to-PSA 10 headline looks dramatic. These percentages describe only the stated example; they are not a forecast for a real card.

sections.heading: Let the evidence decide the length
sections.html:
A shortlist should explain why each exact available copy passes, what could invalidate it and when the evidence was checked. A front photograph, a favourite character or a cheap asking price cannot supply missing sales or condition evidence.

If no copy meets the rules, an empty passing shortlist is a useful result. Research leads can stay labelled as leads without being presented as cleared purchases.

sections.heading: The verdict
sections.html: Keep the gross gap as a discovery filter, then require the net and downside case to work. The example does not pass. Recalculate it yourself before applying the same method to an actual available copy.

articles.title: How to read the TCG Modern Index.
articles.summary: Read the real interface, open the card artwork and follow a dated observation. A visual guide to points, prices, gaps and the source behind them.

sections.heading: The quick take
sections.html:
THE QUICK TAKE

Follow the cards, the dates and the source.

Index points show a basket’s movement on a shared scale. They are not a card’s dollar price or a return after fees.

sections.heading: Read the real screen
Choose the question first
sections.html:
1Index points

A shared starting scale for movement.

2Card price

The individual issue’s own dated guide and currency.

3History window

The actual observed range and eligible basket, shown beside the chart.

The Modern Index’s 2026 trend uses the cards with history from January. Latest lineup uses a more recent shared window. Read the displayed constituent count and dates; neither view promises a full year of observations for every current card.

BlueChip follows its separate high-value lineup. Its longer-history view covers the eligible subset shown on that screen. Earlier prices belong to a selection assembled later, so the chart is retrospective rather than evidence of a basket chosen back then.

sections.heading: Open the actual card
Read the evidence behind the line
sections.html:
Public Raw prices are combined-condition provider market guides, not independently verified individual completed sales. A missing observation stays missing. Retained older observations keep their date. Read each card’s edition and language notes before comparing it with a seller’s copy.

The current public edition keeps PSA 9/10 values pending; pending is unknown, not zero. All three grades are alternatives and must not be added together. TCGCSV documents its archive from 8 February 2024, which limits claims about that source’s earlier history.

A catalogue scan is useful for identification and appreciating art. It cannot prove the condition or value of a specific physical copy offered for sale.

sections.heading: The verdict
sections.html: Use the chart to start a question, then inspect the card and its evidence. Read the source date, basket and gaps before drawing a conclusion. The index is a research view, not a prediction, fund or guaranteed result.

wire.title: Pokémon cards enter the National Toy Hall of Fame
wire.summary: The Pokémon Trading Card Game joined the National Toy Hall of Fame on 5 November, alongside bingo, Care Bears and the playground slide. The four winners came from 12 finalists and are now on view at The Strong National Museum of Play in Rochester, New York. The museum celebrates toys that stay popular across generations and inspire creative play.

wire.title: Pokémon 30th UPC & Delta Reign release day: the queues, the finds and the first rips
wire.summary:
Nine hours outside Smyths, one Delta Reign Elite Trainer Box and one last surprise. UK collector @MunoPepistino said he got home from the queue to an Amazon invitation to buy the 30th Celebration Day box. Over on TikTok, @mersgoth reported a Delta Reign find at Tesco Express. On Threads, @iblisseyy celebrated an Amazon invitation of her own, for a Delta Reign booster box.

The anniversary hunt had its near misses. On X, @phatjer300 said they waited 11 hours, stood 25th in line and still missed out on an Ultra-Premium Collection (UPC). On Reddit, u/IssaLong posted a photo of their Delta Reign haul after striking out on 30th Celebration. FinalScoreFandoms took a camera down the aisles as shoppers hunted for the anniversary box.

Then came the pack rips. Barno Collects Pokémon opened a 30th UPC on YouTube, while @krystalkollectz marked Delta Reign’s arrival with a look back at a decade of Mega Rayquaza pack art. The new releases are separate: Delta Reign brings Mega Rayquaza back, while the anniversary boxes each pack 29 Celebration boosters and a separate three-card Classic Collection pack. Day comes with Espeon ex; Night comes with Umbreon ex.

If you’re still hunting, ask the shop about the exact box before you head out. Finding Delta Reign on the shelf tells you little about whether a Day or Night UPC is still there.
wire.imageAlt: Manga illustration of Alex checking his phone while Oscar and Pikachu wait outside a card shop.
wire.imageCredit: Illustration: BuyTrigger.Cards. Release-day hunt footage: FinalScoreFandoms.

wire.title: Pokémon warns of fake campaign emails in Japan
wire.summary: Pokémon Card Game Japan says spoofed emails are posing as card campaigns and promising money to get people to sign up or log in on fake sites. Pokémon advises deleting the email, avoiding its links and attachments, and entering no personal or payment details. The company says it has found no evidence of a server intrusion or personal-data leak.
wire.imageAlt: Manga-style illustration of a phone displaying an envelope and a warning symbol.

wire.title: Pokémon raises Japan’s five-card booster pack price to ¥230 from May 2027
wire.summary: Pokémon says the suggested price of standard five-card expansion packs released in Japan from May 2027 will rise from ¥200 to ¥230 including tax, up ¥30 or 15%. It cites higher raw material costs among the reasons and says some packs may be priced differently. Hadou Seeker, due 27 November 2026, still lists ¥200.
wire.imageAlt: Manga-style illustration of a foil booster wrapper with a yellow price tag and a rising arrow.

wire.title: Delta Reign launches as Pokémon Center UK sets a new payment deadline
wire.summary: Delta Reign’s tabletop release is dated 6 November. If Pokémon Center UK emailed you on or after 5 November to update a preorder payment, you have until 11:59 pm GMT on 11 November. Pokémon Center estimates it will ship three Delta Reign products in mid-November. Smyths lists the standard Elite Trainer Box and six-pack bundle. We haven’t verified launch-day stock at a named Smyths, Waterstones or Ryman branch.
wire.ctaLabel: Read the UK Delta Reign and UPC guide
wire.imageAlt: Manga-style illustration of a parcel with a clock on its shipping tag.

wire.title: Red RGB Mew auction bidding reaches US$170,100
wire.summary: Bidding for the English red 30th Celebration RGB Mew in a Beckett Pristine 10 Black Label slab reached US$170,100 after 157 bids on 7 November. The same lot stood at US$101,300 after 120 bids on 6 November. The auction remains open: this is a bid, not a completed sale, and excludes shipping and taxes.

wire.title: Gold Rayquaza cools before launch in our eBay sample
wire.summary: The median for ungraded Gold Mega Rayquaza ex 141/103 fell from US$474.50 on 26–31 October (six sales) to US$419.95 on 2–4 November (three sales), down about 11%. We checked exact eBay listings from US sellers at fixed prices, before shipping and tax. The nine sales are a prerelease snapshot.

wire.title: Tacoma card shop offers $5,000 reward after warehouse break-in
wire.summary: A pickup truck smashed through the warehouse entrance at Northwest Sportscards in Tacoma on 2 November. KIRO 7 reports that about US$50,000 in Pokémon and Magic cards was taken. The shop’s owner is offering US$5,000 for information leading to an arrest and is asking other dealers to watch for the stolen stock.
wire.imageAlt: Northwest Sportscards surveillance footage shown by KIRO 7, with a person beside the shop counter.
wire.imageCredit: Surveillance footage: Northwest Sportscards via KIRO 7 News.

wire.title: Alt lists an Expedition Poliwrath PSA 10 sale at US$188,048.
wire.summary: Alt’s result page lists US$188,048 for the 2002 Expedition holo Poliwrath #24, graded 10 by PSA, after 26 bids on 29 October. The auction house highlighted it on 3 November. This is one card’s auction result, not a price for every Poliwrath. Buyer fees and taxes are not itemised on the page.

wire.title: Japan’s next MEGA expansion is dated for 27 November.
wire.summary: The official ハドウシーカー product page lists a 27 November Japanese release, with five cards per pack and a ¥200 suggested retail price including tax. The reveals include Mega Lucario Z ex, Mega Garchomp Z ex and Mega Absol Z ex. These are Japanese product details.
